splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether ERISA's statutory measurement date for withdrawal liability also fixes the deadline for selecting actuarial assumptions. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for thousands of employers in multiemployer pension plans, as the timing of assumption selection directly controls how much withdrawing employers must pay.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions used to calculate withdrawal liability must be selected no later than the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year), providing employers with greater predictability.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that the actuary may select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, allowing the use of more current data even if selected post-year-end.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year and raises questions about judicial power to extend punishment without explicit statutory authorization.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release is tolled during periods of absconding, extending the court's authority to revoke supervised release beyond the original term.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that there is no statutory basis for tolling supervised release during absconding, and the term expires as set in the judgment regardless of the supervisee's flight.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: A longstanding 6-to-3 circuit split exists on whether federal prisoners face the categorical bar of § 2244(b)(1) — which prevents relitigating any previously presented claim — in addition to the separate requirements of § 2255(h). If (b)(1) applies, federal prisoners face a stricter gatekeeping requirement than Congress may have intended for successive collateral attacks.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the categorical bar of § 2244(b)(1) on previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, imposing an additional gatekeeping requirement beyond § 2255(h).

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1) does not apply to federal prisoners' § 2255 motions, meaning they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether candidates can demonstrate a cognizable injury-in-fact sufficient for Article III standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures. The outcome affects how courts evaluate candidate standing to challenge election rules nationwide, with implications for mail-in voting, ballot counting deadlines, and election administration.

positions.label: Candidates have standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates suffer a competitive injury sufficient for Article III standing when a state law allegedly dilutes lawful votes or changes election procedures in ways that affect the electoral outcome.

positions.label: Candidates lack standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates do not have Article III standing to challenge state election procedures pre-election because they cannot demonstrate a sufficiently concrete and particularized injury from ballot-counting rules.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity takes precedence over deference to an agency's interpretation of an ambiguous criminal or sentencing provision (e.g., Auer/Kisor deference to the Sentencing Commission).
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether, when a criminal statute or sentencing guideline is ambiguous, courts should apply the rule of lenity in favor of the defendant or defer to the agency's (or Sentencing Commission's) anti-defendant interpretation. This split has deepened after Loper Bright overruled Chevron and raised questions about the relationship between deference doctrines and lenity.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity prevails over agency deference doctrines when interpreting ambiguous criminal statutes or sentencing guidelines, preventing agencies from using delegated power to expand criminal liability.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency deference (including Auer/Kisor deference to the Sentencing Commission) takes precedence over the rule of lenity, allowing the Commission's interpretation of ambiguous guidelines to control even when it expands criminal liability.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines' commentary (Application Note 1 to § 4B1.2) can expand the definition of 'controlled substance offense' to include inchoate offenses like conspiracy, when the guideline text does not mention them.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether Application Note 1's inclusion of conspiracy and attempt within the career-offender guideline's definition of 'controlled substance offense' is a valid interpretation entitled to deference under Stinson/Kisor, or whether it impermissibly expands the guideline text. This split affects the applicability of the career-offender enhancement to many federal defendants.

positions.label: Commentary validly includes inchoate offenses
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is an authoritative interpretation of the career-offender guideline entitled to deference, and inchoate offenses like conspiracy qualify as controlled substance offenses under § 4B1.2.

positions.label: Commentary impermissibly expands guideline text
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text of § 4B1.2(b) unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses, and Application Note 1 impermissibly expands the definition beyond what the text allows, especially after Kisor narrowed deference.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (all three criminal-history criteria must be met to disqualify) or disjunctive (any one criterion disqualifies).
splits.description: A deep circuit split exists on whether defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief under § 3553(f)(1) only if they meet all three listed criminal-history criteria, or whether meeting any single criterion is disqualifying. This split leads to dramatically different sentencing outcomes for defendants with identical criminal histories depending on the circuit in which they are prosecuted.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), reading 'and' in its natural conjunctive sense.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive or distributive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) is sufficient to disqualify a defendant from safety-valve relief, reading 'and' as distributive or disjunctive.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law (such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to § 924(c)) can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A), and whether the Sentencing Commission's policy statement (U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6)) permitting such consideration exceeds its statutory authority.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether non-retroactive changes in law can be considered as grounds for compassionate release. Some circuits hold that such changes, alone or combined with other factors, can never constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons, while others allow district courts to consider them. The Sentencing Commission's 2024 amendment to § 1B1.13(b)(6) has further deepened this split, with some circuits holding the amendment exceeds the Commission's authority.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in law, whether alone or combined with other factors, cannot contribute to a finding of 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' for sentence reduction under § 3582(c)(1)(A), and that the Sentencing Commission exceeded its authority in § 1B1.13(b)(6).

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider non-retroactive changes in law as part of the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis, particularly when combined with other factors, consistent with the Sentencing Commission's policy statement.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines (U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b)) when the state schedule criminalizes a substance not listed on the federal Controlled Substances Act schedules.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires the substance underlying a state conviction to also be federally controlled. Some circuits hold the definition broadly encompasses any state drug offense regardless of federal scheduling, while others require a federal-law match. This affects career-offender and other sentencing enhancements for many defendants.

positions.label: No federal-law match required
positions.summary: Holds that 'controlled substance offense' under § 4B1.2(b) broadly includes any state drug offense, even if the substance is not controlled under federal law, because the text refers to 'state law' without limitation.

positions.label: Federal-law match required
positions.summary: Holds that a state conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' only if the substance at issue is also controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act, requiring a categorical comparison to federal schedules.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may expressly punish a defendant for the underlying conduct that violated supervised release conditions, or whether revocation sentences must be based solely on the breach of trust.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the permissible basis for supervised release revocation sentences. Some circuits allow courts to consider and punish the underlying criminal conduct that constituted the violation, while others hold that revocation sentences should focus on the breach of the court's trust inherent in violating supervision conditions. The Sixth Circuit's precedent in United States v. Lewis places it at an extreme of this split.

positions.label: May punish for underlying violation conduct
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly consider and punish the defendant for the underlying criminal conduct that constituted the supervised release violation, not merely the breach of trust.

positions.label: Revocation sentences based on breach of trust
positions.summary: Holds that the purpose of supervised release revocation is to sanction the breach of the court's trust, not to punish the new criminal conduct, which should be addressed in a separate prosecution.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners challenging the conditions or terms of their confinement (as opposed to the fact or duration) must proceed through habeas corpus or may bring civil rights claims, and relatedly, whether habeas jurisdiction extends to conditions-of-confinement claims.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether habeas corpus is the exclusive remedy for challenges that affect the terms of confinement but do not directly contest the fact or duration of imprisonment. This split has persisted since the Supreme Court's decision in Preiser v. Rodriguez left the question open, and it affects federal prisoners challenging BOP decisions on matters like First Step Act time credits and prerelease custody placement.

positions.label: Habeas is available for conditions claims
positions.summary: Holds that habeas corpus jurisdiction extends to challenges to the conditions or terms of confinement, including BOP decisions about prerelease custody and earned time credits under the First Step Act.

positions.label: Only civil rights claims (e.g., Bivens) available
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to conditions of confinement that do not contest the fact or duration of imprisonment must be brought as civil rights actions rather than habeas petitions.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of a debtor's property belong to the bankruptcy estate upon a good-faith conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether property appreciation occurring between the original Chapter 13 filing and conversion to Chapter 7 inures to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtor. This split affects the property rights of debtors who convert in good faith and the recoveries available to creditors.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that the broad scope of 'property of the estate' under § 541(a) means that post-petition appreciation inures to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion, not to the debtor.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that under § 348(f)(1)(A), post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation in property belongs to the debtor, consistent with the statute's purpose of protecting good-faith converting debtors.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the civil or criminal appeal deadline applies to appeals from orders on Hyde Amendment motions for attorney's fees in criminal cases.
splits.description: Circuits have split on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees, though filed in a criminal case, is a civil matter subject to the 30-day civil appeal deadline or a criminal matter subject to the 14-day criminal deadline. The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies because the motion is ancillary to the criminal case.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the 30-day civil appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a) applies.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that the 14-day criminal appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b) governs appeals from Hyde Amendment orders because the motion arises in a criminal case.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal documents containing private medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine.
splits.description: Circuits are not uniform on whether denial of a motion to seal medical records constitutes a collateral order subject to immediate appellate review. The D.C. Circuit held that maintaining privacy in medical treatments and diagnoses is a value of 'high order' warranting immediate review, while other circuits have taken different approaches to the collateral order doctrine in sealing contexts.

positions.label: Immediately appealable under collateral order doctrine
positions.summary: Holds that an order denying a motion to seal documents referencing private medical treatments and diagnoses is immediately appealable because medical privacy is a value of high order that cannot be adequately vindicated after final judgment.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that orders denying motions to seal do not satisfy the collateral order doctrine's requirements because they are effectively reviewable after final judgment through post-judgment sealing or other remedies.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c), can constitute or contribute to an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether non-retroactive changes in sentencing law can be considered as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release. Some circuits hold that non-retroactive changes in law can never contribute to such a finding, while others and the Sentencing Commission's 2024 policy statement (§ 1B1.13(b)(6)) allow consideration of such changes. This affects large numbers of federal prisoners serving sentences under now-repealed mandatory minimums.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in law, whether alone or in combination with other factors, cannot contribute to a finding of 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' for a sentence reduction under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may contribute to compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in sentencing law may be considered as one factor among others in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release, consistent with the Sentencing Commission's 2024 policy statement.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether RLUIPA permits suits for money damages against prison officials in their individual capacities. Some circuits allow such suits while others hold that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages, raising questions about the scope of Congressional spending power to impose personal liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA allows individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA authorizes suits for money damages against state prison officials in their individual capacities, as the statute's text is broad enough to encompass such claims.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Landor v. Louisiana Dep't of Corrections

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and Spending Clause legislation cannot impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments under federal civil rights law?
splits.description: The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve disagreement among circuits over the standards for discrimination claims against hospitality and business operators, including questions about liability and available remedies. The Second Circuit's approach was deemed sufficiently unsettled to warrant review.

positions.label: Broader liability standards
positions.summary: Holds that broader standards apply to discrimination claims against business establishments, potentially allowing for more expansive remedies.

positions.label: Narrower liability standards
positions.summary: Holds that narrower standards govern such claims, limiting the scope of liability and available remedies for discrimination in public accommodations.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
